prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Arista Networks, Inc." (ticker ANET), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ANET", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Arista Networks, Inc.
result.industry: Cloud, AI and enterprise networking equipment and software
markets: Data-center and AI Ethernet switching (scale-out and scale-across back-end and front-end networks)
Enterprise campus wired and wireless LAN
Network software, observability and security (EOS, CloudVision, AVA)

mission.plain: Arista wants to build the fastest, most reliable and most programmable networks that connect cloud and AI data centres, campuses and branches, from the client to the cloud.

about.plain: Arista makes the very fast switches and routers that pass data between computers inside huge data centres. When thousands of AI chips need to talk to each other at once, Arista's boxes and software move that traffic. All of its machines run one piece of software, called EOS, which makes the network easier to run and harder to break. It also sells networking gear for offices and campuses.
about.customers: Giant cloud and AI companies such as Microsoft and Meta, plus banks, telecom firms, neoclouds and large businesses.
about.everyday: When you ask a chatbot a question or stream a video, the data likely passes through Arista switches inside a Microsoft or Meta data centre.

money.plain: high-speed data-centre, AI and campus switches and routers
support contracts and CloudVision software subscriptions
Etherlink switches that connect AI GPU and accelerator clusters; 2026 target of at least $3.5B in AI fabrics
office switches, Wi-Fi and VeloCloud SD-WAN (bought from Broadcom in 2025); 2026 campus target of at least $1.25B
routing that links AI data centres in different places; Arista puts this market at $15-20B by 2030

result.summary: Arista has a real competitive advantage: a single, highly reliable software stack (EOS) running on fast merchant-silicon hardware, deep engineering relationships with the largest cloud and AI builders, and a 2Q26 IDC share of 18.7% of data-centre Ethernet switching. Its advantage rests more on product quality, speed of execution and customer intimacy than on lock-in, and it is exposed to two customers (Microsoft 26% and Meta 16% of 2025 revenue), white-box switches and NVIDIA's bundled Spectrum-X networking.

pricingPower.evidence: GAAP gross margin held at 64.1% in 2024 and 64.06% in 2025 even as revenue grew 28.6%, but non-GAAP gross margin slipped to 63.4% in Q2 2026 from 65.6% a year earlier as larger cloud-titan deals and higher memory and silicon costs bit, and management guides 62-64% for 2026; the biggest customers negotiate hard and can switch to white boxes.

moats.evidence: Arista is a Leader in Gartner's Magic Quadrants for data-centre networking (2015-2020) and for enterprise wired and wireless LAN (2026), and its EOS reliability reputation helps win banks and hyperscalers, but it is not a consumer brand.

Customers build automation, monitoring and operations around EOS and CloudVision, and its 10,000+ customers rarely rip out a working network, but the largest buyers deliberately dual-source and data-centre gear is refreshed every few years.
There is little direct network effect, though a growing base of engineers trained on EOS and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium ecosystem help a little.
With $9,006M of 2025 revenue and 150M+ cloud ports shipped it buys merchant silicon (Broadcom) at scale and runs a lean model with a 42.8% GAAP operating margin, but Cisco and NVIDIA are far larger.

The high-end data-centre switching market supports only a few branded vendors (NVIDIA 20.4%, Arista 18.7%, Cisco 18.2% of 2Q26 data-centre Ethernet switching per IDC), but it is large and growing fast enough to attract new entrants and white-box makers.

From 2008 Arista used merchant silicon and one Linux-based operating system for every product, while Cisco relied on custom chips and many operating systems it could not easily abandon; that gap has narrowed as rivals adopted similar approaches.

EOS uses a single binary image and a state-sharing database (SysDB) that isolates faults, built over nearly two decades of software quality discipline; Arista's software and hardware engineering record is hard to replicate quickly.
Co-founders Andy Bechtolsheim (Sun, early Google investor) and Ken Duda and CEO Jayshree Ullal give it unusual engineering talent and hyperscaler relationships, though no exclusive physical asset.

customers.evidence: Microsoft (26% of 2025 revenue, up 67.2%) and Meta (16%, up 40.9%) keep expanding with Arista year after year, the customer count passed 10,000 in 2024 and Etherlink AI networking now has more than 100 cumulative customers.

talent.evidence: Arista is an engineering-heavy company (R&D was $1,237M, or 13.7% of 2025 revenue) led by renowned founders, and it appeared on Glassdoor's Best Places to Work in 2014 and 2015, though it has not featured on recent employer rankings it cites.

product.evidence: Arista is named a Leader with the highest Strength of Offering score in the Forrester Wave for Data Center Network Solutions (Q3 2026) and a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Enterprise Wired and Wireless LAN, and it launched the 7060X-E7 100-terabit platform with 1.6-terabit ports in 2026.

competitors.name: Cisco Systems
competitors.note: Data-centre, AI, campus switching and routing; #1 in Ethernet switching with 28.7% share in 2Q26 (IDC).

competitors.name: NVIDIA
competitors.note: Spectrum-X Ethernet and InfiniBand networking bundled with its AI GPUs; #1 in data-centre Ethernet switching with 20.4% in 2Q26 (IDC).

competitors.name: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (incl. Juniper Networks and Aruba)
competitors.note: Data-centre switching, routing (Juniper, acquired 2025) and campus Wi-Fi/switching (Aruba, Mist).

competitors.name: Celestica
competitors.note: White-box data-centre switches built for hyperscalers, which can replace branded switches.

competitors.name: Accton Technology
competitors.note: White-box (ODM) data-centre and AI switches for cloud giants.

competitors.name: Huawei Technologies
competitors.note: Data-centre, campus switching and routing, mostly outside the US; 8.2% of Ethernet switching in 2Q26 (IDC).

competitors.name: Nokia
competitors.note: IP routing for service providers and data-centre switching (SR Linux), boosted by its Infinera purchase.

competitors.name: Dell Technologies
competitors.note: PowerSwitch data-centre switches, often running SONiC, sold with AI servers.

competitors.name: New H3C Technologies (Unisplendour)
competitors.note: Data-centre and campus networking in China.

competitors.name: Fortinet
competitors.note: Secure SD-WAN and campus switches/Wi-Fi bundled with firewalls.

competitors.name: Broadcom
competitors.note: Arista's main chip supplier (Tomahawk, Jericho), whose merchant silicon also powers white-box rivals.

threats: Customer concentration: Microsoft (26%) and Meta (16%) made up 42% of 2025 revenue, so a capex pause by either would hit growth.
NVIDIA bundling Spectrum-X Ethernet with its GPUs; it overtook Arista as #1 in data-centre Ethernet switching in 1Q26 (IDC).
White-box switches from Celestica and Accton running SONiC or in-house software at hyperscalers.
Cisco and HPE-Juniper competing harder in AI networking and campus after consolidation.
Dependence on Broadcom merchant silicon and tight supply of chips and memory, which squeezed gross margin to 63.4% non-GAAP in Q2 2026.
Shifts in AI architecture, such as co-packaged optics or scale-up fabrics (NVLink), that could favour vertically integrated vendors.

ceo.name: Jayshree Ullal
ceo.background: Electrical engineering degree (San Francisco State University) and master's in engineering management (Santa Clara University); former Cisco senior vice president of data-centre switching

c1.evidence: Arista is one of the two or three leaders in AI and cloud data-centre networking (18.7% of data-centre Ethernet switching in 2Q26 per IDC), a market IDC says grew 64.5% year on year to $12.3B in that quarter.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Arista for EOS's reliability and programmability, open merchant-silicon hardware and close engineering work with cloud titans, an advantage built over 18 years, but NVIDIA, Cisco and white-box makers are closing gaps.

c3.evidence: Arista is a default choice among network engineers and cloud builders, but ordinary people have rarely heard of it, unlike Google or NVIDIA.

c4.evidence: Arista's founding vision to 'revolutionize high-speed Ethernet at massive scale' and its 'client to cloud' message are consistent and engineering-driven, but it does not publish a widely known mission statement.

c6.evidence: “reliable, high-performance, AI networking” is the typical impression among investors and engineers, which is mostly positive, while the general public largely does not know the name.

c7.evidence: Arista targets a $105B addressable market by 2029 riding AI and cloud build-outs, and IDC's data-centre Ethernet switch market grew 64.5% in 2Q26.

c8.evidence: It has expanded from data-centre switching into campus (2026 target at least $1.25B), routing, SD-WAN through the 2025 VeloCloud purchase, and scale-across AI networking it sizes at $15-20B by 2030.

m1.evidence: Jayshree Ullal has pushed Arista from cloud networking to 'Arista 2.0' AI, campus and client-to-cloud platforms, and she was early to call Ethernet's win over InfiniBand in AI back-end networks.

m2.evidence: Ullal is not a founder but has led Arista since 2008, before its first product shipped, and she runs it with founder-like long-term focus alongside co-founders Andy Bechtolsheim and Ken Duda.

m4.evidence: Ullal stresses customer-first engineering and quality, and big customers keep expanding their spending, but there is little public evidence of an explicit servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Arista's culture of software quality around a single EOS image and close hardware-software co-design has kept launching new platforms, such as the 2026 7060X-E7 1.6-terabit switch.

m6.evidence: Ullal is an electrical engineer who ran Cisco's data-centre switching business and stays deeply involved in product and technology strategy.

m7.evidence: Ullal is respected and has no public scandals, but there is little public evidence on whether her stewardship aims at a purpose beyond building a great company.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Jayshree Ullal at a top university such as Stanford, Harvard or MIT could be found.

m8b.evidence: Ullal is a well-known, forthright and colourful presence on earnings calls (for example 'Arista 2.0'), but she does not have the cult public profile of Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: Under Ullal revenue grew from $2,317.5M in 2020 to $9,005.7M in 2025 while the GAAP operating margin rose from 30.2% to 42.8%, and 2026 guidance was raised to about $12.6B.

m10.evidence: Arista runs lean, with 2025 sales and marketing of only $533.4M (5.9% of revenue) and G&A of $141.9M (1.6%), though it is not famous for symbols of frugality.

c10.evidence: Its networks underpin cloud services and AI used by billions of people via customers like Microsoft and Meta, but the benefit is indirect and Arista is invisible to end users.

p2.evidence: Building switches that move 1.6-terabit-per-port traffic among hundreds of thousands of AI accelerators without failure is extremely hard and is critical to AI and cloud computing.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin rose from 30.2% in 2020 to 42.8% in 2025, but gross margin was roughly flat (63.9% in 2020 vs 64.1% in 2025, dipping to 61.1% in 2022).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Arista had $13,343.3M of cash and marketable securities, no debt and $14,797.7M of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $699.7M (2020) to $3,856.1M (2025); operating cash flow rose from $735.1M to $4,371.9M but fell to $492.8M in 2022 as inventory was built.

v1.evidence: Arista is widely regarded as having the most reliable, programmable data-centre switch software, but NVIDIA's Spectrum-X bundle and Cisco's breadth mean it is not clearly the best for every buyer.

v2.evidence: Arista was a Glassdoor Best Places to Work in 2014 and 2015 and a Bay Area News Group Top Place to Work in 2019, but it does not appear on recent major employer rankings.

c5.evidence: Cloud and AI operators such as Microsoft, Meta and many banks would notice quickly, as their networks rely on Arista's switches, though alternatives exist and ordinary users would not see it directly.
